newsitem.title: UK: THAI ASSET QUALITY PROBLEMS SEEN COSTLY -- S&P.
newsitem.headline: THAI ASSET QUALITY PROBLEMS SEEN COSTLY -- S&P.

text.p: Substantial asset quality problems in the banking system are at the heart of Thailand's financial turmoil and pressure on the baht, Standard & Poor's sovereign ratings managing director David Beers said on Friday.
In an interview with Reuters Financial Television, Beers said the full magnitude of the asset quality problem had only now started to feed through.

"Even with the government's decision to allow the baht to depreciate, which ought to actually cushion some of the blow to the economy, it is evident that the losses are going to be much larger than were foreseen earlier in the year, and that in turn is what is going to be costly to the government.
"Our concern is what this is going to cost the government in terms of bailing out the system," he said.
On August 1, S&P placed Thailand's "A" long-term foreign currency rating on creditwatch with negative implications. S&P said about $3.0 billion of foreign currency debt was affected.

The creditwatch placement reflected greater than expected loan losses in the financial sector which were expected to put a sizeable fiscal burden on the government and lead to weakened economic growth for several years, it said.
"Any time you have a rating on credit watch negative the message we're conveying to the market is that its possible that the rating will fall," Beers told RFTV.
At the same time S&P placed the ratings of eight financial institutions from Thailand on negative creditwatch.
S&P said the rating action reflected concerns that non-performing loans and loan losses would rise to levels not consistent with current ratings.
The Thai baht drifted lower on Friday awaiting the conclusion of Monday's loan talks with the International Monetary Fund's (IMF), dealers said.

Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya will leave for Japan on Sunday to meet the IMF and other institutions as well as about 10 potential donors including the United States and Japan to secure loans to stabilise the troubled Thai economy.
Thailand is seeking $12-$15 billion in international loans to get its economy back on an even keel.

"The crucial issue is to what extent the fund can help the government take decisive action...there are some key reforms and steps that we are looking for in the IMF programme which will help us decided whether and to what extent the rating should fall," Beers said in the RFTV interview.
Korea also has an asset quality problem in its banking system, Beers said.

"Longer term there is an intriguing question as to what would happen if there is reunification between north and south Korea and that story looks to us to be heating up a bit," he said. -- Hayley Pienaar, London Newsroom +44 171 542 7718
